About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Business and Economics Year 11 of
the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Business and Economics Year 11 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Business and Economics Year 11 is proposed
to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Business and Economics Year 11 will be required to start using it in Year 11
from 1 January 2028.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Business and Economics, students are taught how businesses, consumers,                     Year 11 Business and Economics leads to further study in Business Studies,
  and governments interact in the economy. Students are taught how to apply                     Economics, and other related subjects in Years 12 and 13.
  financial and economic reasoning and use economic models to explain decision-
  making in context. Students are also taught how internal operations and external
  influences affect business operations, and how economic theory connects to
  practical business concepts, such as marketing, people management, business
  planning, and operations management.


Students are taught core business and economic concepts, models, and systems,
including scarcity, opportunity cost, resource allocation, business purpose, business
processes, and decision-making. They use this disciplinary knowledge to understand,
explain, and interpret economic and business activity within local, national, and global
contexts.

Business and Economics provides students with the knowledge and practices to
analyse economic and business issues, situations, data, and systems in both
contemporary and theoretical contexts. Students apply disciplinary concepts, models,
frameworks, and evidence to investigate patterns, relationships, influences, and
impacts, using economic and business reasoning to explain outcomes, evaluate
decisions, and explore implications.

As students progress through Year 11, they develop the ability to evaluate
information, synthesise perspectives, and communicate well-reasoned conclusions
using disciplinary language, concepts, and evidence in written form. This enables
them to justify decisions, develop recommendations, and participate thoughtfully in
economic, business, civic, and community contexts while considering ethical, social,
cultural, environmental, and long-term implications.

                           The circular flow model is used to illustrate the relationships between, and the
                            interdependence of, the five sectors of the economy: households (consumers),
                            businesses (firms/producers), the government, financial institutions, and the
                            overseas sector.
                           The circular flow model shows how money moves in an economy, and how
                            economic events impact on the money flows (payments) and real flows (goods,
                            services and resources provided) between the sectors:
                            o households provide labour (real flow)
                            o businesses pay wages (money flow)
                            o businesses provide goods and services (real flow)
                            o households spend money (money flow).
                           Injections are flows of money into the circular flow that are outside of household
                            and business spending. These include government spending (G), investment (I),
                            and export receipts (X). Withdrawals are flows out of the circular flow, namely
                            through taxation (T), savings (S), and import payments (M).
                           Economic growth is an increase in the real value of goods and services
                            produced, usually measured by growth in gross domestic product (GDP). It leads
                            to an expansion of income, output, and spending in the circular flow.
                           Sustained economic growth occurs when productive capacity increases through
                            improvements in the quantity and quality of resources and higher productivity,
                            allowing the economy to produce more goods and services over time.
                           Government economic policies can influence the circular flow and growth in an
                            economy. Fiscal policy refers to government decisions about its spending
                            (injections) and taxation (withdrawals).
                           The difference between government spending and revenue is the budget
                            balance, which can be a surplus or a deficit. A deficit occurs when spending is
                            greater than revenue and is usually financed by borrowing, which must be repaid
                            in the future.

                            customer, in which the seller identifies the customer's need, communicates the
                            value of the product or service, and responds to questions or hesitation to
                            support a purchasing decision.
                           Feedback from the target market, including what the target market asks,
                            respond to, or decline, particularly in a direct selling situation, provides direct
                            evidence of whether a promotional strategy and the solution are meeting the
                            needs of the target market.
                          Finance
                           The finance function is responsible for planning and reporting financial
                            information, including funding, budgeting, and monitoring inflows and outflows to
                            support business decision-making.
                           A budget is a financial plan predicting expected revenue and costs before a
                            period, while an income statement summarises actual revenue, costs, and profit
                            after a period. Variance analysis compares these two to identify differences and
                            inform future decisions.
                           Break-even analysis identifies the level of sales at which total revenue equals
                            total costs, resulting in zero profit. The margin of safety measures how far actual
                            or expected sales exceed the break-even point, indicating the level of risk in
                            business operations.
                          Operations
                           The operations function transforms inputs (e.g. labour, materials, and
                            equipment) into outputs (e.g. goods and services), influencing the cost, quality,
                            and efficiency of production. Productivity is a measure of how efficiently this
                            transformation occurs, expressed as output divided by input. Labour productivity
                            measures output per worker or per hour worked.

                           Businesses are required to meet a range of tax obligations, including declaring

                            reaches a specified threshold, and maintaining accurate financial records to
                            support timely and correct payments to the relevant government authority.
                           When a business employs staff, it takes on additional obligations including
                            deducting and passing on employee tax contributions, levies, and retirement
                            savings scheme contributions on behalf of their employees, and maintaining
                            accurate records of these deductions.

                            business.

                           Businesses operate within a legal framework that protects consumers, promotes
                            honest trading, and safeguards personal information; meeting these obligations
                            is fundamental to customer trust, credibility, and long-term viability.
